text:
Semester 5 Startup Project
A student prototype for finding, swapping, and reusing wearable clothes.
Prepared by: Project Team
A campus-focused website where students list wearable clothes and find items from other members.
Members request a direct swap or use internal credits to balance an exchange. Both sides confirm the handover.
Make clothing exchange easier and more affordable while giving usable clothes another owner.
A simple exchange flow for a familiar campus problem
Students may have wearable clothes they no longer use, while other students want affordable variety. Finding a suitable person to exchange with can be difficult.
Students and campus communities looking for low-cost clothing and convenient local exchanges.
“When I have clothes I no longer wear, help me find someone nearby who wants them so I can exchange them easily and safely.”
The project starts from the clothing reuse and affordability problem. Student demand still needs to be checked through interviews or a campus pilot.
Students in one campus or nearby student community. This is a starting hypothesis, not a measured market size.
Affordable options, clear item photos and condition, local exchange, and simple requests.
General resale marketplaces and social media groups can help people find clothes, but they are not designed around a campus exchange flow.
A small local community, direct swaps, and internal credits for balancing exchanges. User interviews and competitor research should validate this difference.
Strengths and risks at the prototype stage
Campus-focused exchange flow. Direct swaps and internal credits. Working student prototype.
Demand is unvalidated. Exchanges depend on local members. Pro pricing and features are only proposals.
Pilot with campus clubs. Learn from swap events. Test optional Pro features after free use is understood.
Low listing activity, unsafe handovers, misleading item details, privacy incidents, and larger resale platforms.
Proposed model for a student prototype

text: Start with free exchanges, then test optional revenue
A campus-focused C2C exchange. Members list items and arrange exchanges with each other through the website.
Browsing and exchanging remain free. Internal credits are prototype points and have no cash value.
A future experiment could offer optional listing or alert features at ₹49 per month or ₹399 per year. The prices and demand are unvalidated.
A campus swap event could explore sponsorship. There is no current revenue, payment gateway, or live payment processing.
React and TypeScript website with a Java 21 Spring Boot backend and relational data model.
Create an account, browse or list clothing, request an exchange, and confirm the handover.
Ask students about trust, item condition, sizes, preferred exchange points, and whether they would list or request items.
Run a small supervised campus pilot, gather feedback, and improve listing quality, reporting, privacy, and safety guidance before wider use.

text: Build and maintain the website, Java API, database, and user flows.
Talk with student groups, prepare launch information, and invite pilot members.
Set exchange guidance, review reports, and help members resolve handover issues.
Track project costs, document assumptions, and coordinate responsibilities. One student may cover more than one role.
Items to review before a real launch
Closet Cycle is a student prototype. No company registration, tax registration, or government recognition is claimed.
If the project becomes a business
Choose an appropriate legal structure with qualified advice and check applicable registration and tax duties.
Privacy notice, terms of use, listing rules, reporting process, and clear exchange or cancellation guidance.
Record who owns the brand, code, images, and project materials. Use only photos and content the team has permission to use.
Responsive web prototype built with React, TypeScript, and Vite.
Java 21 with Spring Boot and a relational database design.
Clothing listings can show category, size, condition, description, and photos.
Cloud hosting and production deployment are planned items. AWS is not deployed. Review the mobile experience and accessibility before a pilot.
A local exchange replaces shipping in the prototype
Member requests an item, both sides agree, they arrange a suitable campus handover, then confirm completion.
Internal credits only help balance exchanges. They are not money and cannot be purchased or withdrawn.
UPI, card, and net banking options are mock interface elements only. No payment data or money is collected.
Members currently arrange handovers themselves. No warehouse, shipping partner, or reverse-logistics service is active.
Campus clubs, sustainability groups, student societies, and opt-in social channels. These are proposed channels, not confirmed partners.
Explain how listing, requesting, credits, and handover work. Use real sample listings only with permission.
Invite a small group, encourage referrals, and share swap event details if a campus host agrees.
Track sign-ups, complete listings, exchange requests, completed handovers, and member feedback during the pilot.
Trust comes from clear listings and reliable exchanges
Show accurate photos, condition, size, and clear descriptions.
Use request status and two-sided confirmation. Give members practical guidance for public handover locations.
Provide a way to report a listing or member and explain how moderators review reports.
Use saved searches or alerts as possible Pro features only after demand is validated. Ask members what would make them return.
Student prototype with no current revenue and no live payment processing.
Development time, domain and hosting, database and image storage, security, moderation, and any payment-provider fees if payments are later enabled.
Optional Pro at ₹49 monthly or ₹399 yearly, plus possible event sponsorship. Neither has been tested or earned revenue.
Estimate actual hosting and operating costs, survey willingness to pay, and test a free campus pilot before setting a break-even target.
Outside factors that could affect Closet Cycle
Campus rules may affect promotion, events, and exchange locations. Any public support or grant would need confirmation.
Students may be price-sensitive. Hosting and moderation still cost money, while Closet Cycle has no current revenue.
Members may like affordable reuse, but trust, sizing, condition, and safe meetups affect participation.
The prototype depends on secure accounts, reliable hosting, and image storage. Production deployment is still planned.
Reuse may keep clothes in use longer. The project has not measured waste or emissions impact.
Privacy, user terms, intellectual property, and future payment rules need review before a real launch.
Learn on one campus before expanding
Complete core flows, review privacy and safety guidance, recruit a small pilot group, and prepare sample listings.
Run a limited campus trial. Observe whether members list items, request exchanges, and complete handovers.
Use feedback to fix confusing steps, weak listings, reporting gaps, and accessibility issues.
Expand to another campus only after the first pilot shows repeat use and the team can support moderation and hosting.
Practical safeguards for a responsible exchange
Few listings can make the platform feel empty. Start with a small, coordinated pilot and measure completed exchanges.
Incorrect condition details, no-shows, or unsafe handovers can harm trust. Use clear listing rules, reporting, and public-location guidance.
Collect only needed data, restrict access, protect accounts, and review security before production.
Clothing reuse may extend garment life, but Closet Cycle has not measured waste reduction or emissions. Avoid impact claims until measured.
A focused campus pilot is the next step
Closet Cycle gives students a simple place to find and exchange wearable clothes within a local community.
A student prototype and proposed backend structure show the core idea and exchange flow.
Validate demand, run a supported campus pilot, review safety and privacy, then decide which features and business model are worth building.
If students use it and the team can operate it responsibly, Closet Cycle could support more campus communities.
